CELEBRATE THE REAL THING

Little milestones, honestly counted.

Everything on this shelf comes from something your child really did — a class finished, a game played, a picture saved. Nothing here is a score, and nothing is shared anywhere: it is your room, on your device.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 30 cards in Classroom, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Classroom. We have 30 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Backpack

    “Backpack! This is your backpack. Where does it go? On your back! What goes inside? Snack — in! Bottle — in! A picture you made — in! Zip, zip. Off we go!”

    How: Pack the real bag together tonight: one thing to eat, one thing to drink, one thing to show. Each item goes in with its name — "snack… in!" — and the zip click ends the ritual. Same time every evening, and packing becomes your child’s job, not yours.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Notebook

    “Notebook! Open the notebook. A page for you, a page for me. Draw a line… draw a circle… look what the pencil did! Turn the page — more paper waits!”

    How: Start a two-minute notebook habit: one page a day, anything your child likes — scribbles, circles, a letter they are working on. Date the corner for them. In a month, flip back to page one together and count how the marks changed.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Pencil

    “Pencil! The yellow pencil. Pinch it near the point — thumb, finger, finger. Make a dot… a line… a wiggle! The pencil talks when your hand moves.”

    How: Try "pencil races": you draw a slow line, your child draws a fast one; you draw a circle, they try one. Big paper, fat grip, no corrections — the goal is a hand that wants to come back tomorrow, not a perfect letter today.

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Crayons

    “Crayons! Open the box. Red… blue… green… yellow! Which one today? Push the paper — look, COLOR! The crayon paints with your hand.”

    How: Pick three crayons and play color match: one scribble on paper, then hunt for one real thing in the room that color. Red scribble — find red! Three rounds is a full game, and it clears the table of every crayon but three.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Eraser

    “Eraser! The rub-a-dub block. Oops went wrong? No tears — rub, rub, rub… and the paper is blank again! Try again. That is what the eraser is for.”

    How: Draw a wobbly line on purpose, hand over the eraser and let your child rub it out — the rubbing itself is excellent hand work. Then say the magic sentence together: "wrong lines are how right lines start."

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Ruler

    “Ruler! The straight-edge stick. Hold it flat… line it up… draw along the edge — a STRAIGHT line! Wiggle the ruler, draw again — a new straight line!”

    How: Go on a straight-line hunt: find three straight things in the room (the table edge, a book, the floor tiles), lay the ruler along each, then draw one straight line of your own. Curvy things are allowed too — the ruler just says no to them politely.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Scissors

    “Scissors! Thumb on top, two fingers below — open… close… open… close! The scissors only cut paper. Sit down to cut. Slow snips make the line.”

    How: Sit side by side and cut a strip of paper into scraps — the snipping matters more than the shape. Say the rules out loud each time: paper only, sitting down, walking never. Grown-up eyes stay close by the whole time, and the scissors live up high afterwards.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Glue

    “Glue! Twist the cap… round and round. Dot, dot, dot on the back — press it down… push… pat! Stuck! The glue holds your art together.”

    How: Tear an old magazine page into pieces and glue the pieces into a new picture — tearing and pressing are both good hand work. One dot per piece keeps the sticky mess friendly; a "dot, dot, not a lot" chant keeps it that way.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Desk

    “Desk! This is the work desk. Sit down, feet flat, paper ready. At the desk we draw, we build, we write. All done? Push in the chair — the desk says thank you!”

    How: Name one spot at home "the desk" — the kitchen table corner counts perfectly. Work happens there, one activity at a time, and the crayons live in a cup on it. Same spot every day turns "time to work" into an easy sentence.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Chair

    “Chair! Sit on the chair. Bottom on the seat, feet on the floor, back tall like a tree. Look — sitting like a big kid! The chair holds you while you work.”

    How: Play "show me sitting": chair, floor, cushion — which one is the sitting spot? Then sit for one short story and stand up when it ends. Sitting well is a skill with a finish line, not a rule for the whole day.

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Teacher’s Desk

    “Teacher’s desk! The big desk. Whose desk is it? The teacher’s! Papers live here, stickers live here, the plan for the day lives here. It is polite to knock and ask.”

    How: Pretend play is the game: your child sits at a table being the teacher, you raise your hand and ask a question. Swapping roles lets a child see the room from the other side — and teachers-in-training suddenly love rules.

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Whiteboard

    “Whiteboard! The big board. A marker for the grown-up… what shall we draw? A sun! A two! Your name! Rub, rub — all gone! The whiteboard waits for the next idea.”

    How: Big paper works as a home whiteboard. Draw giant letters together — arm movements first, then marker strokes — and let your child wipe it "clean" with a cloth. Wiping is the reward, and it is also serious hand work.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · Bookshelf

    “Bookshelf! The book house. Books stand up here like friends on a shelf. Pick one… sit down… open it slowly. Finished? The book goes back in its spot, ready for tomorrow.”

    How: Turn one shelf at home into the bookshelf: books standing, spines out, at your child’s own height. The game is the return trip — story finished, book back in its slot. A shelf a child can reach is a shelf a child will use.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · Globe

    “Globe! The whole world, tiny! Here is the water — so blue. Here is the land — so green. Spin it slowly… round and round, just like the Earth does. Where are we? Right here!”

    How: Spin the globe (or the map on a screen), stop it with a finger, and name whatever is under it — ocean, land, ice. Then find your own home and put a sticker on it. One sticker, one place, one very proud child.

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Map

    “Map! The world on paper. The blue is water. The green is land. Point to the water… point to the land… point to where we live! A map knows where everything is.”

    How: Hang any map at child height and play "point and name": one finger, one place, one word each. Draw a small star where grandma lives, another where you live. Two stars make the map personal — and then it gets looked at every day.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · Clock

    “Clock! Round and round. The long hand runs fast, the short hand walks slow. When the hands say twelve, we eat lunch! When they say three, we tidy up!”

    How: Tie the clock to one real moment a day — "when the big hand is up top, snack time!" Say it, wait for it, celebrate when it arrives. One learned moment turns the clock from wall decoration into a promise.

  20. 18
    Card 17 · Computer

    “Computer! The big screen. We sit down, we take turns, we use it for a little while. Type a letter… hear the sound… watch the story. All done — screen closes, off we play!”

    How: Decide the rule before the screen turns on: what we will do, for how long, and who gets the first turn. A timer makes the ending easy — the timer finishes the turn, not the grown-up saying stop.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · Wastebasket

    “Wastebasket! The scrap bin. Paper bit… in it goes! Snip, snip, done? Walk it over… drop… in! The wastebasket says thank you. The room stays lovely.”

    How: Make clean-up the finishing move of every craft: one basket, one walk, one drop, a small cheer. Who can land the scrap in from one step back? A shot that scores makes tidying the best part of the project.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · Listen

    “Listen! Hand to your ear. What do you hear? The story… the birds… a quiet room. Ears open, mouth quiet, eyes on the book. Now I know you are listening!”

    How: Play the listening game: whisper an instruction across the room — "touch your nose… hop twice… bring the red block." Whispering makes ears work. Then swap: your child whispers, you do the silly move.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Raise Your Hand

    “Raise your hand! Arm up high — like this! When your hand is up, the teacher sees: ‘this friend has something to say!‘ Wait for the nod… and now it is your turn to talk.”

    How: Practise at home at story time: anyone with a thought raises a hand and waits to be picked. Make the waiting short and the picking generous — "yes, you wanted to say something!" The habit sticks when turns come round honestly.

  24. Cards 21–30
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Follow Directions

    “Follow directions! Ears ready? ‘First hang your coat, THEN come to the rug.‘ Coat… rug… all done! Two steps, both done — that is following directions!”

    How: Give two-step missions at home: "put the cup on the table, then sit down." Count the steps on fingers before starting. Two steps done in order earns a high five — then tomorrow, sneak in a third.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · Be Kind

    “Be kind! A helping hand, a friendly word, a gentle touch. Someone fell? Help them up. Someone is sad? Sit close. Kind hands, kind words — that is how friends are made.”

    How: Catch kindness in the act: whenever your child helps, shares or comforts, name it out loud — "that was kind!" Kindness that gets noticed gets repeated. One caught moment a day is plenty.

  27. 24
    Card 23 · Share

    “Share! One book, two friends. You hold it first… my turn to turn the page… now your turn! Taking turns IS sharing. Look how far one book goes.”

    How: Share something real: one colouring page with two crayons, one puzzle, one book with two laps. Say the turn out loud — "your page, my page" — and swap on a count of ten. Fair, short, repeat.

  28. 25
    Card 24 · Help Others

    “Help others! See a friend stuck? ‘I can help!‘ Two crayons fall — pick one up, hand one back. Helping makes the job small and the friend happy. High five, helpers!”

    How: Make your child the household helper once a day: carrying the spoons to the table, passing the pegs while you hang washing, holding the door. Real helping — the kind that actually helps — is what builds the identity of "I am a helper."

  29. 26
    Card 25 · Say Please

    “Say please! ‘Can I have a snack… PLEASE?‘ There is the magic word! When you say please, asking sounds kind — and kind asks are the ones that get a yes.”

    How: Play the polite-request game at pretend shops and tea parties, where every order needs a please to be served. Then catch it for real: a genuine "please" at the table gets warm praise and, nearly always, the snack.

  30. 27
    Card 26 · Say Thank You

    “Say thank you! Someone gave you a crayon? ‘Thank you!‘ Grandma brought a story? ‘Thank you!‘ Hand on your heart, big smile — thank you makes the giver happy too.”

    How: Make thank-you the end of every exchange for one day: snack, help, a passed ball — each one gets its thank you. Then at bedtime, remember together: who did we thank today? Two remembered thank-yous is a lovely day.

  31. 28
    Card 27 · Use a Quiet Voice

    “Use a quiet voice! Finger on lips… shhh. Inside, we use our inside voice — soft and low. Outside? Loud voices, go! But right now we are inside… shhh… can you hear the quiet?”

    How: Play the voice dial: outside voice on the balcony or in the yard, middle voice in the hall, whisper voice in the car. Name the voice before entering each place — "library voices now!" — and let your child show you the difference.

  32. 29
    Card 28 · Walk

    “Walk! Inside we walk — one foot, other foot, steady like this. Running feet? Those are for the garden and the park! Inside… walk, walk, walk. Safe and proud.”

    How: Practise the switch: at the door, "running feet ready… walking feet ON!" Then walk a straight line together, heel to toe, like tightrope explorers. Make the walking itself the fun part and the rule takes care of itself.

  33. 30
    Card 29 · Clean Up

    “Clean up! The game is done — now the blocks go home. Block in the box… book on the shelf… crayons in the cup. Sing the clean-up song… look! The room is ready for tomorrow.”

    How: Clean up together the first hundred times — never alone. Make it a race against a song, sort by color as you go, and finish with a look-around: "who made this room lovely? YOU did." One basket per toy type makes the whole thing possible.

  34. 31
    Card 30 · Keep It Tidy

    “Keep it tidy! One paper out, one paper done, one paper away. The pencils sleep in the cup, the books stand on the shelf. A tidy desk says: ready for tomorrow!”

    How: End each work session with the tidy look: crayons cupped, paper stacked, chair pushed in. Snap a photo of the tidy desk once a week — a tidy-spot gallery your child will be proud to grow.

  35. 32
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  36. 33
    Check

    “Can you find Backpack? Now show me Clock.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  37. 34
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 30 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
